title: What is psychotherapy and what does it involve?
intro: Psychotherapy, or talking therapy, is a treatment for mental health problems and emotional difficulties. A trained therapist works with you through conversation and exercises to understand and change thoughts, feelings and behaviour. It is effective for conditions such as depression, anxiety, trauma and many others.

sections.heading: Main approaches
paragraphs: Cognitive behavioural therapy focuses on thoughts and behaviours and is structured and practical. Psychodynamic therapy explores past experiences and unconscious patterns. Humanistic and systemic approaches focus on personal growth and relationships. Other methods include trauma-focused therapy, interpersonal therapy and mindfulness-based programmes. The best method depends on the problem and person.

sections.heading: What sessions are like
paragraphs: Sessions usually last fifty minutes, weekly or every few weeks, individually, as couples, with families or in groups. The therapist listens, asks questions and suggests ways of coping, and you may do exercises between sessions. Therapy can last from a few sessions to a year or more. What you say is confidential, with legal exceptions concerning serious risk.

sections.heading: Does it work
paragraphs: Research shows that psychotherapy helps many people, and benefits often last longer than medicines alone. The relationship with the therapist is among the strongest predictors of success. Therapy requires effort and time, and may bring up difficult feelings before improvement. Medicines and therapy are sometimes combined.

sections.heading: Finding a therapist
paragraphs: Look for a licensed professional, such as a psychologist, psychiatrist or psychotherapist. Check what insurance covers and whether waiting lists exist. A first meeting helps to see whether you feel comfortable. Online therapy is also available and works for many people. In an emergency or with thoughts of self-harm, seek urgent help right away.

sections.heading: Making the most of it
paragraphs: Be open and honest, set goals, try the exercises, and talk about it if therapy is not helping. You may change therapist if the fit is poor. Progress is often gradual.

examples.title: Choosing a therapist
examples.text: Imagine you want help with anxiety. You could book short first meetings and choose the therapist you trust most.

examples.title: Practising between sessions
examples.text: Suppose your therapist gives breathing exercises. You might practise daily and report what worked at the next session.
